title: Degradation rootcause: warm cache + precision blend review
summary: Customer seeing intermittent quality regressions after switching to an INT8+AWQ deployment in their VPC. Symptoms: deterministic queries OK, but live traffic shows ~8-12% NLU score drop after cold-starts and during short traffic bursts. Team suspects KV cache warmup + layerwise precision mixing interactions. Session enumerates hypotheses, repro plan, logs to collect, and a staged mitigation (sticky warm caches + canary with precision gating).
topics: Repro and bisect plan, short-term mitigations
action_items: Diego Ramos - produce layer-level activation diffs for top 50 failing prompts - due 2028-05-13
Tara Nguyen - export 1000 failing request traces (input+pinned seed) and share S3 link - due 2028-05-11
Priya Nair - run controlled canary with sticky KV mode and report latency impact - due 2028-05-12
Samir Patel - provide VPC flow logs and packet loss metrics for the last 48h window - due 2028-05-10
next_steps: Redwood to send quantization checklists, layer-probing script, and a sample config for sticky KV cache
Customer to run repro harness with deterministic seeds and attach model artifacts
Schedule a follow-up triage on 2028-05-16 to review bisect results
transcript:
Meeting: 2028-05-09 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lin (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Eng); Samir Patel (Aurelia ML), Ellen Zhou (SRE), Harold Kim (Head ML), Tara Nguyen (Data Scientist)
Shared artifacts: deck: https://redwood.app/decks/aur-quant-review (shared), benchmark sheet: https://s3.amazonaws.com/aur-repro/quant-bench.csv (customer), diagnostics script: redwood-layer-probe.py (attached)

Summary (auto): quick technical deep dive on accuracy regressions after quantization rollout to INT8+AWQ in VPC. Focus on cache warmup, layerwise performance, and mitigations (precision gating & sticky KV).

[00:00] Maya Lin: Hey everyone, thanks for carving this time. Uh, the plan is to go through what you're seeing, walk through the hypotheses, and land on a repro + mitigation plan. Samir, do you wanna start with the observed failure modes?
[00:28] Samir Patel: Yeah thanks Maya. So, quick context — we rolled INT8+AWQ for the 13B variant last week in our VPC deployment, right. We used Redwood's recommended profile, enabled continuous batching and standard KV caching. Initially things looked fine, deterministic evals passed, but in production we started to see a drop in our intent-class F1 for about 8 to 12% on a subset of queries. It mostly happens after cold-starts or traffic spikes.
[00:59] Ellen Zhou: To add, we're seeing the drop correlate with when workers spin up and KV cache is, uh, cold. Also some pods were restarting around 02:00 UTC due to a node upgrade, so I think there's interplay.
[01:18] Diego Ramos: Okay, that's helpful. When you say deterministic evals passed — do you mean unit test prompts that you run locally with fixed seeds?
[01:26] Samir Patel: Yes. We ran your quant validation harness and the reference prompts gave near-identical logits. The live diffs show divergence after a few tokens in the response.
[01:36] Priya Nair: Interesting — divergent after a few tokens indicates KV cache or past-key-value divergence. Could be cache staleness, or mismatch in cache priming with AWQ's per-layer activation scaling.
[01:49] Harold Kim: We also tried toggling batching low to see if throughput interactions were causing non-determinism. Lower batching reduced latency but didn't completely fix the accuracy drop.
[01:59] Maya Lin: Right. Let's enumerate hypotheses. I'll throw several on the table: (1) true quantization regression in certain layers that only shows up with live prompt distribution, (2) KV cache warmup/staleness where the cached KV shapes or quantization parameters mismatch, (3) batching/ordering causing non-deterministic token generation, (4) a network/VPC artifact causing partial pops in KV fetches, or (5) a rollout misconfiguration mixing FP and quantized model shards.
[02:29] Tara Nguyen: We also noticed more regressions on prompts with long context (700+ tokens) and with lots of repeated system tokens. Could be KV eviction thresholds.
[02:40] Diego Ramos: Good note. AWQ and GPTQ both do per-channel/ per-layer scale factors. If KV cache stores quantized KV with one scale and then a later runtime path expects a slightly different scale (say after re-compilation or kernel selection), you can get subtle biases that grow token-by-token.
[02:58] Ellen Zhou: Is that a known problem with warm caches? Because on restart the runtime sometimes recompiles kernels — we saw compilation events in the logs.
[03:07] Priya Nair: Yep, kernel selection/compilation can change the execution path. Usually semantically equivalent but floating rounding/noise with INT8 can amplify.
[03:15] Samir Patel: We also have HSM/KMS for key rotation and some audit agents, could that add latency and cause partial KV timeouts?
[03:23] Maya Lin: It could. Timeouts leading to missing cached KV might cause the runtime to fallback to compute path intermittently; mixing cached vs compute could give answers with different numeric histories. We'll want to look at the server and application logs for KV cache hits/misses correlated with the failing requests.
[03:41] Harold Kim: For repro, Tara exported a set of 1,000 live failing requests with seeds and timestamps and uploaded to our shared bucket. We can start there.
[03:51] Tara Nguyen: yes link is in the sheet. we also attached traces with the sequence of pod ids during generation. some runs show the pod switching mid-generation.
[04:02] Diego Ramos: Pod switching mid-generation is a smoking gun — if the request is proxied and hops between instances with different model builds/profiles, that's very likely to produce divergence. Do you use sticky sessions?
[04:12] Ellen Zhou: No, we left the default LB behavior. We assumed the Redwood runtime would handle a seamless fallback, but we did notice occasional 'KV priming failed' warnings around the same timestamps.
[04:23] Priya Nair: Ok, so immediate mitigation: enable sticky affinity for the canary; that'll ensure the same worker handles generation end-to-end. Also enable the 'sticky_kv' mode in the runtime (we'll provide the sample config) so KV cache remains local for a generation session. That reduces cross-worker staleness.
[04:40] Samir Patel: Sounds good. But we also want to understand why deterministic tests don't fail. Any idea?
[04:46] Diego Ramos: Deterministic harnesses often use shorter contexts and single-worker runs — they don't exercise the distributed caching, kernel re-compilation, or network variance. Live traffic has bursts, multiple workers, and sometimes different kernel selection due to runtime heuristics.
[04:58] Maya Lin: Let's drill into the per-layer hypothesis. Diego, can you explain the layer-probing approach?
[05:03] Diego Ramos: Sure. We run the same input through the float baseline and the quantized build and capture activations per layer (pre-attn, post-attn, MLP inputs). We then compute per-layer L2 diff and relative bias. If we see a concentrated spike in a small subset of layers (often early MLP layers), that's suggestive of layer-specific quantization sensitivity. If diffs accumulate slowly across layers, it points to KV/floating rounding accumulation.
[05:31] Tara Nguyen: Do you need the entire model artifact or just a trimmed graph?
[05:36] Diego Ramos: For local probes, we can instrument just the forward pass; model weights and scale parameters are needed. We can also do a light-weight probe where we only dump intermediate key/value tensors.
[05:45] Samir Patel: We'll share a download link for the model weights (private bucket) and we've already generated some activation dumps for 20 failing cases.
[05:53] Maya Lin: Good. Now about heuristics — you mentioned adaptive precision gating earlier. Explain how that fits.
[05:59] Priya Nair: Adaptive precision gating is where we use a cheap classifier to decide per-layer or per-token whether to use quantized path or fallback to higher precision (FP16/FP32) for specific timesteps or layers. It adds overhead but can avoid quality cliffs. It can be done as canary: enable gating for top-3 sensitive layers and see if regressions disappear.
[06:18] Harold Kim: That sounds promising but what's the latency hit?
[06:22] Priya Nair: Likely 5-15% depending on how many layers are forced to FP. That's why we prefer sticky KV + canary sticky sessions first to remove the operational source of divergence.
[06:32] Ellen Zhou: On the topic of kernels, our logs had 'chosen kernel: kernel_v2_fast_int8' and later 'kernel: fallback_fp16' in some runs. Why would kernel change mid-run?
[06:43] Diego Ramos: Could be dynamic kernel selection based on observed sequence length or memory pressure. If memory bumps, the runtime may switch to a different kernel for subsequent tokens. That kernel's quantization rounding might differ.
[06:53] Maya Lin: Action: collect kernel selection trace per request. We need time-aligned kernel changes with token offsets. Diego we can provide the instrumentation.
[06:59] Diego Ramos: I'll share a small tracer that logs kernel id, kv_hit boolean, and worker id at each token step. That will help correlate.
[07:08] Samir Patel: Great. A question on AWQ vs GPTQ — is AWQ more likely to introduce per-token drift?
[07:15] Priya Nair: AWQ favors asymmetric weight quant, which can give better average performance but is sometimes more brittle for certain activation distributions. GPTQ's per-row quant tends to be stable for MLP layers but larger memory. In practice, you can see different failure modes. The team should try both on a small canary to compare.
[07:32] Tara Nguyen: We already tried GPTQ earlier and observed slightly higher latency, but didn't dig into production patterns. We can re-run GPTQ on the same canary.
[07:40] Diego Ramos: Also run FP8 experimental (if allowed in VPC) for comparison — FP8 often reduces numeric noise vs INT8 but may have different kernel availability.
[07:48] Ellen Zhou: Is FP8 even supported in our on-prem stack? Our PCI drivers are a bit old.
[07:54] Priya Nair: We'll check kernel compatibility; if drivers are too old, FP8 code paths might fallback or fail. We'll include a compatibility checklist in the follow-up email.
[08:03] Samir Patel: Ok, can we clarify the immediate data to collect? You mentioned traces, activation dumps, kernel logs, and pod mappings. Anything else?
[08:11] Maya Lin: Also capture: kv cache hit/miss counts per request, compilation events, and the full prometheus span for latency per token. And collect the runtime's per-token pseudo-random seed if applicable.
[08:22] Harold Kim: We'll attach network interface metrics too — packet drops, retransmits.
[08:27] Diego Ramos: One more instrumentation: store the quantization scale factors attached to KV when it's written. I want to see if the stored scale matches the expected scale on read.
[08:36] Tara Nguyen: How invasive is that? Will that bloat the logs?
[08:39] Diego Ramos: It's a small dump per KV write — not for all traffic, just for the failing canary or on a sampling rate.
[08:46] Maya Lin: Let's talk timeline: short-term mitigations (within 48h) and medium-term (1-2 weeks). Short-term: enable sticky sessions, enable sticky_kv, reduce canary batch size to minimize cross-worker hops. Medium-term: run layer-probes, bisect model precision, and test adaptive gating.
[09:01] Samir Patel: On sticky sessions — are there pitfalls? We worry about hotspotting.
[09:07] Priya Nair: Hotspotting is a risk if traffic is not evenly distributed; to mitigate, use session-duration TTLs and fallback routing. We'll give recommended TTL of 30s for sticky sessions during the canary.
[09:18] Ellen Zhou: Also, can we do a roll-forward denser canary with weighted routing, 10% of traffic?
[09:23] Maya Lin: Yes. Start with 1% then step to 10% if stable. Always keep telemetry.
[09:28] Tara Nguyen: For the layer-probe diffs, are you expecting to see huge L2 diffs or subtle drift?
[09:33] Diego Ramos: Often it's subtle — relative diffs of 1e-3 in early layers that compound to large decoding differences. But if we see a single layer with a spike (e.g., relative 0.1), that could indicate a bad quant pass on that layer.
[09:45] Harold Kim: Are there any past incidents of kernel mismatches causing production regressions you can point to?
[09:49] Maya Lin: We had a case at a different customer where a micro-update to the runtime changed a fused-kernel path and INT8 rounding rules — it caused decoders to pick different top tokens after five tokens on average. The fix was to pin kernel versions and add a kernel compatibility check during deploy.
[10:05] Samir Patel: Let's talk about reproducibility: some failing requests are non-deterministic across retries. How do we best capture that?
[10:12] Priya Nair: Capture the whole request event: input text, model version, worker id, token-by-token logits (or top-k logits), kernel ids, kv_hit booleans, and seeds. Then rerun the same event in a single-worker isolated environment. If it reproduces, you can bisect.
[10:27] Maya Lin: Ok, for the bisect plan: (A) run layer-probe to find suspect layers, (B) selectively force those layers to FP16 and run canary, (C) if still failing, try switching quant method (AWQ->GPTQ->FP8) on those layers, (D) as last resort, consider model shard pinning so all shards use same quant profile.
[10:45] Tara Nguyen: Forcing layers to FP16 — how intrusive is that in the runtime config?
[10:49] Diego Ramos: We support a 'layer_precision_map' in the serving config where you can list layer ranges to override. It's hot-reloadable on the canary fleet. We'll provide an example.
[10:58] Samir Patel: Excellent. On security/compliance: we need to ensure the diagnostic dumps don't leak PHI — some of these prompts include clinical notes. We will anonymize prior to sharing but will need the team to support a redaction workflow.
[11:11] Maya Lin: Absolutely. For any dataset you share, please scrub or provide hashes. Redwood can run the probes on-prem on your infra if you prefer — we can bring a private troubleshooting image. We'll discuss the on-prem option if needed.
[11:24] Harold Kim: One sticky thing — our devops noted that when we disabled auto-recompile, some latency increased by 10% but kernel stability improved. Is that acceptable?
[11:34] Priya Nair: For the canary, yes. For long-term, we'd prefer a stable kernel selection matrix with performance guarantees. We'll help tune compilation heuristics.
[11:43] Ellen Zhou: Are you concerned about quantization seeds? I mean, model initialization seeds?
[11:48] Diego Ramos: Quantization itself is deterministic given the same calibration dataset and RNG, but some code paths use stochastic rounding or pruning. If stochastic rounding is enabled, that could introduce run-to-run variance. We'll check the quant config used during offline conversion.
[12:01] Samir Patel: We'll attach the quant conversion logs.
[12:05] Maya Lin: Ok, let's capture concrete next steps and owners — Diego will produce the tracer and layer-probe script and run initial analysis on the 20 dumps and the 1k failing traces Tara shared. Priya will share the sticky_kv config and layer_precision_map sample. Samir/Ellen will run the sticky canary and share logs. We'll reconvene on 2028-05-16 for results.
[12:25] Tara Nguyen: Quick note — our NG firewall team also discovered a 0.2% packet drop during the upgrade window. Could that be enough to cause partial KV fetches?
[12:33] Diego Ramos: Yes, if KV fetches cross the network (e.g., in remote caching mode) and partial responses happen, it's possible. We should confirm whether KV is local-only or remote-backed in your current config.
[12:44] Samir Patel: We're using a mixed mode — local with remote fallback for eviction.
[12:49] Maya Lin: Then network artifacts could definitely amplify. Short-term: force local-only KV for the canary to eliminate network variables.
[12:58] Harold Kim: Will that increase memory pressure?
[13:01] Priya Nair: Possibly, but for a small canary it's fine. We'll help estimate memory.
[13:07] Ellen Zhou: Any other diagnostic flags to enable?
[13:10] Diego Ramos: Enable 'detailed_token_trace' and 'kernel_trace' at 1% sample rate. Also increase sampling of KV telemetry to 5% during the canary.
[13:20] Maya Lin: Great. Anything else from the customer side?
[13:23] Samir Patel: One more ask — if layer-probe shows a single faulty layer we may want a hotfix to just re-quant that layer. How quickly could Redwood provide that?
[13:33] Diego Ramos: If it's a single layer, and we can reproduce it, we can produce a re-quant artifact and a hot patch in a few days, assuming no infra blockers.
[13:41] Tara Nguyen: ok good. We'll prioritize the 1000 traces upload and the anonymized prompts. Expect the link in the sheet by EOD.
[13:49] Maya Lin: Perfect. We'll send an email with the checklist: instrumentation to capture (kernel_trace, kv hits, worker ids), links to the scripts (layer-probe, tracer), and the sticky_kv sample config. Also propose the 2028-05-16 follow-up.
[14:01] Harold Kim: Thanks everyone.
[14:04] Maya Lin: Thanks — we'll talk soon.

Notes (imperfections): occasional mislabels in the transcript, 'KV cash' appears once in an auto-transcribe block; some technical names like AWQ/GPTQ are sometimes spelled 'AWQ' and 'G P T Q' in the raw. There are filler words and overlapping talk at ~04:00-04:10 where pod switching was discussed.
